title: Missingness-Aware Learning for Downstream Tasks in Tabular and Time-series Data
Abstract
text:
Data missingness shows up in many real-life scenarios, arising from different sources like improper data collection, malfunctioning equipment, or operational data loss. In all these scenarios, imputation, which is the process of filling data gaps with estimated values, is a widely accepted approach to complete missing data for machine learning and deep-learning tasks such as classification and regression. For instance, biomedical data frequently suffers from extensive missingness due to patient behavior, poor data management, and biased sampling, which complicates downstream analyses like patient stratification.
However, it is well-known that all types of imputation induce biases in the data that can negatively impact the downstream task, and recent work has shown that improvements in the quality of imputation do not necessarily result in improvement in downstream task performance. In particular, the quality of imputation decreases when the size of the dataset is small. In this thesis, I will focus on datasets with small sample sizes, which for example arise very often in real-world scenarios. Small datasets can in particular reduce the quality of simple imputation due to sampling error, especially in the case of heterogeneous features.
In this thesis, I will explore techniques to incorporate the objective of downstream tasks explicitly into learning with missing data. For this, I first look at K-Nearest Neighbours (kNN) imputation on tabular data. Secondly, I look into short time series data with regular structural missingness. Finally I look at missingness in graph-structured data. First I argue that nearest neighbor-based imputation methods can outperform advanced deep neural network-based and generative approaches. In particular, I derive theoretical guarantees for the quality of kNN imputation under different missingness scenarios. I then introduce Fast Iterative Improvement for Imputation (F3I) as a modification of the kNN approach with a novel loss function, that nevertheless preserves those same theoretical guarantees. Furthermore, I show that jointly training a hyperparameter-tunable loss function that forms a homotopy between the imputation and downstream objectives can further improve downstream task performance, thereby going beyond the conventional impute-then-classify paradigm. Secondly, I consider settings where the missingness is structurally regular, such as in short multivariate time series with missing time points or missing features. For these problems, I develop Multivariate Functional Linear Discriminant Analysis (MUDRA) to show that discretization-invariant feature extraction and classification based on functional data analysis techniques can outperform the classical impute-then-extract features paradigm. Finally, I consider missing labels in more complex structured data, such as graph-structured datasets. I then develop a method called Fast Semi-Supervised Node Embedding via Structural and Label-Aware Optimization (FUSE) to show how the inherent local and global community structures of the network can be used to construct informative node features for imputing the missing labels, in a more accurate and computationally efficient manner than random walk or mutual information-based formulations. 
These results demonstrate that imputation quality alone should not be the sole criterion for evaluating and constructing missing-data methods for real-life applications. Since imputation is ultimately performed to facilitate downstream analysis, the objectives of the downstream task should be explicitly incorporated into the design and evaluation of learning algorithms on missing data. This can be achieved either by jointly optimizing imputation and downstream objectives, as in the proposed loss-based F3I approach, or by bypassing imputation altogether when the structure of the data permits, as in the functional data analysis-based approach MUDRA. More broadly, this thesis advocates for a task-oriented perspective on missing data, in which the success of an imputation method is ultimately determined not only by how accurately it reconstructs missing values, but also by how effectively it supports the downstream task.

title: Zusammenfassung
text:
Datenfehlzeiten treten in vielen realen Szenarien auf und lassen sich auf verschiedene Ursachen wie fehlerhafte Datenerfassung, defekte Geräte oder operationellen Datenverlust zurückführen. In all diesen Szenarien ist die Imputation, bei der Datenlücken durch geschätzte Werte gefüllt werden, ein weithin akzeptierter Ansatz zur Vervollständigung fehlender Daten für Aufgaben des maschinellen Lernens und des Deep Learnings wie Klassifikation und Regression. Beispielsweise leiden biomedizinische Daten häufig unter umfangreichen Fehlern aufgrund von Patientenverhalten, mangelhaftem Datenmanagement und verzerrter Stichprobenziehung, was nachgeschaltete Analysen wie die Patientenstratifizierung kompliziert.
Es ist jedoch hinreichend bekannt, dass alle Arten von Imputationen Verzerrungen in den Daten hervorrufen, die sich negativ auf die nachgeschaltete Aufgabe auswirken können, und neuere Arbeiten haben gezeigt, dass Verbesserungen der Imputationsqualität nicht zwangsläufig zu einer Verbesserung der Leistung der nachgeschalteten Aufgabe führen. Insbesondere sinkt die Qualität der Imputation bei geringer Datensatzgröße. In dieser Arbeit konzentriere ich mich auf Datensätze mit kleinen Stichprobengrößen, wie sie beispielsweise sehr häufig in biomedizinischen Kontexten auftreten. Kleine Datensätze können insbesondere die Qualität einfacher Imputationen durch Stichprobenfehler verringern, vor allem bei heterogenen Merkmalen.
In dieser Arbeit argumentiere ich, dass auf dem k-nächste-Nachbarn-Verfahren basierende Imputationsmethoden fortschrittliche Ansätze auf Basis von Deep Neural Networks und generative Ansätze übertreffen können. Insbesondere leite ich theoretische Garantien für die kNN-Imputation unter verschiedenen Fehlerszenarien her und modifiziere das kNN-Imputationsparadigma durch die Einführung einer neuartigen Verlustfunktion, die es uns dennoch ermöglicht, diese theoretischen Garantien aufrechtzuerhalten. Darüber hinaus zeige ich, dass das gemeinsame Training einer hyperparameterabstimmbaren Verlustfunktion, die eine Homotopie zwischen den Imputations- und den nachgeschalteten Zielen bildet, die Leistung der nachgeschalteten Aufgabe weiter verbessern und somit über das konventionelle Imputate-dann-Klassifiziere-Paradigma hinausgehen kann. Ich betrachte auch Szenarien, in denen die Fehlselbstständigkeit strukturell regulär ist, wie etwa bei kurzen multivariaten Zeitreihen mit fehlenden Zeitpunkten oder fehlenden Merkmalen. Für diese Probleme demonstriere ich, dass diskretisierungsinvariante Merkmalsextraktion und Klassifikation auf Basis von Verfahren der Funktionalen Datenanalyse das klassische Paradigma des Imputierens vor dem Extrahieren von Merkmalen übertreffen können. Schließlich erweitere ich die Diskussion über Fehlwerte auf fehlende Labels in komplexeren strukturierten Daten, wie etwa graphenbasierten Datensätzen, im Rahmen desselben Fehlermodells, das in der Imputationsliteratur verwendet wird. Ich zeige, wie die inhärente lokale und globale Community-Struktur des Netzwerks genutzt werden kann, um informative Knotenmerkmale für die Imputation der fehlenden Labels zu konstruieren, und zwar auf eine präzisere und recheneffizientere Weise als bei Formulierungen, die auf Random Walks oder gegenseitiger Information basieren.
Diese Ergebnisse zeigen, dass die Imputationsqualität allein nicht das einzige Kriterium für die Bewertung und Konstruktion von Methoden für fehlende Daten sein sollte. Da die Imputation letztendlich zur Erleichterung der nachgeschalteten Analyse durchgeführt wird, sollten die Ziele der nachgeschalteten Aufgabe explizit in das Design und die Bewertung von Imputationsmethoden einfließen. Dies kann entweder durch die gemeinsame Optimierung von Imputations- und nachgeschalteten Zielen erreicht werden, wie bei dem vorgeschlagenen verlustbasierten kNN-Ansatz, oder durch das vollständige Umgehen der Imputation, wenn es die Struktur der Daten erlaubt, wie bei dem auf der Funktionalen Datenanalyse basierenden Ansatz. Im weiteren Sinne plädiert diese Arbeit für eine aufgabenorientierte Perspektive auf fehlende Daten, bei der der Erfolg einer Imputationsmethode letztendlich nicht nur daran gemessen wird, wie genau sie fehlende Werte rekonstruiert, sondern auch daran, wie effektiv sie die nachgeschaltete Aufgabe unterstützt.

Chapter 3  Error Guarantees for Nearest-Neighbor Imputation

Reintroduce nearest neighbour imputation, and state objective to modify it for downstream task
Argue why it is better than Bayesian methods in maintaing alignment with data, show high probability concentration bounds for imputed values.
Introduce Fast Iterative Improvement for Imputation (F3I) and the novel objective function. Argue why a differentiable function makes it easier to modify and optimise for downstream task.
Present PCGradF3I.
Result: kNN / Random Forest imputation chained with an MLP outperforms more advanced deep-learning architectures and are more robust.
Conclusion: reiterate that better imputation does not necessarily mean better downstream task performance. Argue for the need of methods to perform downstream tasks without imputation.

Restate problem with imputation according to [1]
Introduce the multivariate time-series classification problem.
Present Multivariate Functional Linear Discriminant Analysis (MUDRA) [2] to perform dimension reduction and classification without imputation.
Show how classification performance is improved over LOCF imputation
Show how imputed values closely align with ground truth
Results: Downstream tasks performed without imputation outperforms training on simple imputation methods
Conclusion: We talked about missing values on tables, and missing values on multivariate time series. Now we introduce missing values on graph clustering, a more complicated data structure.

Chapter 5  Fast Semi-Supervised Node Embedding via Structural and Label-Aware Optimization

State the semi-supervised learning problem on graphclustering: learning when labels are missing, which means modularity cannot be directly calculated
Show how to use the graph structure to generate representations even with missing modularity, by imputing labels so as to increase the modularity of the remaing graph
Show how the labels can then be reconstructed time-efficiently.
Results: Semi-super

Chapter 6  Conclusion

Conclude that missing values are best dealt with without imputation
The more complicated the underlying data structure, the more information to be gleaned to bypass imputation.
Marginal gains in imputation are not worth it, instead imputation should be moderated by downstream task performance in order to get the best results.

title: 1  Challenges with Missing Data
text:
1.1 Motivation for dealing with missingness
In most statistical and machine learning literature, datasets are assumed to be complete. For instance, in case of tabular data, it is assumed that all features are observed for each sample. Similarly, in the case of multivariate time-series data, it is often assumed that all features for each sample are measured at the same time points. In practice however, datasets are often incomplete, with some features unobserved for certain samples, or fragmented in case of time-series data, with observations or features missing at different time points across samples.
A similar issue is label missingness, which has given rise to the field of semi-supervised learning. Label missingness refers to the scenario where only some samples in the dataset are labeled. However, approaches to semi-supervised learning often assume similar distribution of the missing labels as the available labels, which is often not reflected in real world scenarios. An example for this is the task of anomaly detection, where often only some positive samples are labeled and the unlabeled part of the dataset consists overwhelmingly of non-anomalous samples.
In this chapter, I will introduce the different types of missingness that has been proposed in the literature, as well as propose a new classification of missingness based on a different perspective. I will also discuss how the semi-supervised setting can be viewed as a special case of missing data, and how it can be incorporated into the overall missingness framework.

title: 1  Challenges with Missing Data
text:
1.1.1 Missing data in the real-world setting and Challenges - Missing attributes 
A common example of incomplete and fragmented data in the biomedical data is electronic health records. Patients usually have different lengths of stay in a hospital, and are prescribed different medical tests depending on their symptoms. Compiling this data into a single dataset usually results in extensive missingness across features and time points, resulting in an incomplete, fragmented and sparse data structure. For example, in [1] the collected dataset records longitudinal bone density data of 423 individuals from 9-26 years of age. Although measurements for all individuals span almost 18 years of age, measurements were actually made for each individual at most four times, typically across less than 5 years. This causes the dataset to be highly fragmented in the time domain. Similarly, a prominent real-life benchmark in multivariate time series research is the Beijing Multi-Site Air Quality dataset [2], which exhibits sporadic missing features and irregular temporal alignment across monitoring locations.


1.1.2 History of simple unsupervised imputation - constants, measures of central tendency, extremums, etc.
Imputation is defined as the procedure of filling in missing or null values in a dataset with substituted values. One of the earliest structured approaches to imputation comes from agricultural data [3]. The problem here is the analysis of the effect of various fertilisation treatments on different plots of land, where data for the effect of some treatments on some plots is not available. Under the classical single factor ANOVA framework, the missing values are imputed by minimizing the variance of the yield conditioned on the general, block-specific and treatment-specific means. In general, the approach to imputation advocated here is to find the value which minimizes the squared sum of the errors between the true and estimated yields.
One of the first structured analyzes of different types of imputation approached comes from the discipline of survey methodology [4]. This work looks at the statistical properties of imputed values for nine different types of imputation, for three different scenarios in which data can be missing [5]. This includes a form of K-Nearest Neighbours (kNN) imputation, which is described as “distance function matching” here.

1.2 Notation


1.2.1 Mathematical formulation
Throughout this thesis, I will use the standardised notation encouraged by most machine learning conferences. Italicized letters will indicate deterministic quatities. Normal small letters indicate numbers (\(x,y,t\)), bold small letters indicate vectors (\(\vx,\vy,\vt\)), bold capital letters indicate matrices (\(\mX,\mY,\mT\)), capital letters in sans-serif fonts indicate tensors \((\tX,\tY,\tT)\) and blackboard bold capital letters indicate sets (\(\sX,\sY,\sT\)) (with the exception of \(\E\) and \(\P\) which are defined below). The non-italicized versions of these indicate random quatities; random variables are \(\rx,\ry,\rt\), random vectors are \(\rvx,\rvy,\rvt\) and random matrices are \(\rmX,\rmY,\rmT\). Elements of higher order arrays like vectors, matrices, and higher order tensors are denoted by regular versions of the bold letters with subscripts: \(\evx_1,\emX_{11},\etX_{111},\ervx_1,\ermX_{11}\), etc. For a matrix \(\mX\), \(\mX_{i,:}\) and \(\mX_{:,i}\) will denote the \(i^{th}\) row and column respectively.
When two random variables \(\rx\) and \(\ry\) are independent, I will denote that as \(\rx\independent\ry\).
I will denote the vectorization of a matrix \(\mX\), which means stacking the columns of the matrix sequentially, as \[\vec(\mX)=[\mX_{:,1}^\trans\quad\mX_{:,2}^\trans\quad\cdots\quad\mX_{:,n}^\trans]^\trans\] The determinant of a matrix \(\mA\) will be denoted by \(|\mA|\), and Kronecker product of two matrices \(\mA_{m\times n}\) and \(\mB_{p\times q}\) is an \(mp\times nq\) matrix defined as \[
\mA\kron\mB\deff\begin{bmatrix}
\emA_{11}\mB &\emA_{12}\mB&\cdots\emA_{1n}\mB\\
\emA_{21}\mB &\emA_{22}\mB&\cdots\emA_{2n}\mB\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
\emA_{m1}\mB &\emA_{m2}\mB&\cdots\emA_{mn}\mB\\
\end{bmatrix}
\] The generalized psedo-inverse [6, p. 20] of a matrix \(\mA\) will be denoted by \(\mA^-\), which simply indicates that \(\mA\mA^-\mA=\mA\). It should be clear that the choice of \(\mA^-\) is not unique for a singular matrix \(\mA\), i.e. if \(|\mA|=0\). In cases where a unique choice is necessary, I will use the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse [7] \(\mA^+\), which is defined by the following properties: \[\mA\mA^+\mA=\mA\qquad\mA^+\mA\mA^+=\mA^+\qquad(\mA\mA^+)^*=\mA\mA^+\qquad(\mA^+\mA)^*=\mA^+\mA\].
I will denote the probability of an event \(E\) as \(\P(E)\), expectation of a random variable \(\rx\) as \(\E[\rx]\), its variance as \(\Var(\rx)\), and its covariance with another random variable \(\ry\) as \(\Cov(\rx,\ry)\). I will denote the variance-covariance matrix of a random vector \(\rvx\) as \(\Var(\rvx)\). For a matrix \(\mSigma\), \(\norm{\rvx}_\mSigma\) will denote the Mahalanobis norm [8] of \(\rvx\) with covariance \(\mSigma\), defined as \(\norm{\rvx}_\mSigma\deff\rvx^\trans\mSigma^-\rvx\).
I will also denote the KL divergence of 2 distributions \(P\) and \(Q\) over the support \(\sX\) as \[\KL(P||Q)\deff\int_{x\in\sX}P(x)\log\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}dx\] The Cartesian product of two sets \(\sA\) and \(\sB\) will be denoted by \(\sA\times\sB\).

text:
1.3 Problem Formulation (Add more discussion about the definitions, to motivate to non-experts)
I will adopt notation similar to [9] for the problem formulation and denote missing values as NaN. Let \(\rvx\in \sX=(\sX_1\times\ldots\sX_D)\) be a D-dimensional random vector. The entries of this random vector can be continuous (\(\sX_d=\R\)) or categorical (\(\sX_d=\{1,\ldots,K_d\}\)) random variables, for \(d\in\{1,\ldots,D\}\). We do not have complete observational access to \(\rvx\); instead our observation is mediated by a random masking vector \(\rvm\in\{0,1\}^D\). If \(\ervm_d=1\), then \(\ervx_d\) is observed. Assume that \(\rvm\) follows a distribution \(\pmask\), and the data \(\rvx\) follows a distribution \(\pdata\).

title: 1  Challenges with Missing Data
text:
1.4 Types of missingness
Classical literature mainly distinguishes three main missingness mechanisms depending on the relationship between the probability of missingness with the observed and unobserved data [5]. These can be distinguished based on the form and properties of \(\pmask\).

1.4.1 Missing Completely at Random (MCAR)
MCAR is a missingness mechanism where the probability of missingness is independent of the observed and unobserved data. In other words, the missingness is completely random and does not depend on any of the observed or unobserved data. This is equivalent to the statement that \(\rvx\independent\rvm\). This also indicates that each component of \(\vm, m_i\), is an independent Bernoulli random variable with probability \(p_i\) independent of \(\vx\).
